claims.text: Increasing chromium content in steel promotes formation of a stable Cr2O3 passive layer under corrosive conditions.
The Cr2O3 passive layer is self-healing.
The Cr2O3 layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
Formation of the Cr2O3 barrier reduces the corrosion rate of steel in environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The proposed controlled study varies primarily chromium content while maintaining well-characterized steel microstructures.
The intervention is to vary steel chromium content and expose all samples to a controlled corrosive environment.
A continuous and adherent Cr2O3 layer is the proposed structural mediator.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes under corrosive conditions to form Cr2O3.
The Cr2O3 film limits diffusion of oxygen and other corrosive species to the underlying metal.
Limiting transport of corrosive species through the Cr2O3 film slows further corrosion.
Higher-chromium steels are predicted to have significantly lower corrosion rates than minimal-chromium baseline steels under identical exposure conditions.
Higher-chromium steels are predicted to exhibit lower corrosion-related weight loss than the baseline.
Higher-chromium steels are predicted to exhibit improved electrochemical corrosion properties relative to the baseline.
The predicted corrosion improvement should coincide with a continuous protective Cr2O3 layer detectable by surface analysis.
The protective behavior is expected to hold only under conditions supporting passive-film stability, including temperatures below 300°C, controlled pH, and moderate chloride concentrations.
Extreme pH, very high temperature, or highly aggressive ionic strength may prevent the same protective behavior.
The chromium threshold for protection and the magnitude of corrosion-rate reduction may depend on other alloying elements and environmental conditions.
The proposed experiment compares nominal chromium levels of 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% while holding other alloying elements constant.
Corrosion is to be assessed using weight loss, electrochemical impedance measurements, and XPS/SEM characterization of oxide composition and continuity.
The hypothesis is falsified if higher chromium produces no statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction or no detectable continuous Cr2O3 layer under passivating conditions.
